1. Heard Mr. Divyansh Tiwari, learned counsel for the
petitioner  and  Ms.  Astha  Sharma,  learned  counsel
appearing for the respondent/applicant.
2. Delay condoned.
3. In IA No.291609 of 2026 – a joint application has
been  filed for  directions under  Article 142  of the
Constitution of India in a disposed of Transfer Petition.
The Transfer Petition was disposed of on 30th August 2022.
By the said order, this Court transferred the proceedings
pending between the parties from Jalandhar, Punjab and
Ghazipur, Uttar Pradesh to the Patiala House Courts,
Delhi.
2

## Page 91

4. The peculiar fact which has led to the filing of
the joint application for divorce in this Court is that
when the parties approached the Patiala House Courts with
an application under Section 13-B of the Hindu Marriage
Act, 1955, objections on jurisdiction were raised.
5. The marriage between the parties was solemnized on
7th June, 2017 and they have been living separately for
the last 7 years.
6. In view of the peculiar facts of the case and this
Court having already exercised jurisdiction to transfer
the cases and the parties being now handicapped from now
filing  a  petition  under  Section  13-B  of  the  Hindu
Marriage Act, 1955 in Delhi, we are inclined to entertain
the joint application filed for dissolution of marriage
here.
7. The  parties  have  entered  into  a  Settlement
Agreement dated 1st June, 2026. The terms and conditions
of the Settlement Agreement are as under:

1. That the parties to this deed entering this settlement deed at their own

3. That the first two parties undertake to file the first motion for mutual
divorce under Section 13B(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 within one

agreement.

9. At the outset, we have no hesitation to record that the decisions in
Indorama Synthetics (India) Ltd.  (supra)  and  Tayal Cotton Pvt.
Ltd. (supra) cannot be called in aid to support the contention advanced
by Mr. Dave. Those decisions arose in the context of Section 446 of the
Companies Act and Section 14 of the IBC, respectively. The statutory
provisions  falling  for  consideration therein  operate  in  different milieu
whereas Section 5 of the SARFAESI Act is intended to achieve a distinct
object. The reasoning in those decisions, therefore, cannot govern the
interpretation of the specific provisions falling for consideration in the
present case. We  record  that the  High Court was  right  in not  being
guided thereby in arriving at its conclusions.

11. An informed decision on the question of law arising for decision would

20 5. Acquisition of rights or interest in financial assets.—(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any agreement
or any other law for the time being in force, any asset reconstruction company may acquire financial assets of any bank
or financial institution,—
(a) by issuing a debenture or bond or any other security in the nature of debenture, for consideration agreed

may be agreed upon between them; or
(b) by entering into an agreement with such bank or financial institution for the transfer of such financial assets
to such company on such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between them.
(1-A) Any document executed by any bank or financial institution under sub-section (1) in favour of the asset
reconstruction company acquiring financial assets for the purposes of asset reconstruction or securitisation shall be
exempted from stamp duty in accordance with the provisions of Section 8-F of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 (2 of 1899):
Provided that the provisions of this sub-section shall not apply where the acquisition of the financial assets by
the asset reconstruction company is for the purposes other than asset reconstruction or securitisation.
(2) If the bank or financial institution is a lender in relation to any financial assets acquired under sub-section
(1) by the asset reconstruction company, such asset reconstruction company shall, on such acquisition, be deemed to be
the lender and all the rights of such bank or financial institution shall vest in such company in relation to such financial
assets.
(2-A) If the bank  or financial institution is holding any right, title or interest upon any tangible asset or
intangible asset to secure payment of any unpaid portion of the purchase price of such asset or an obligation incurred or
credit otherwise provided to enable the borrower to acquire the tangible asset or assignment or licence of intangible
asset, such right, title or interest shall vest in the asset reconstruction company on acquisition of such assets under sub-
section (1).
(3)  Unless  otherwise  expressly  provided  by  this  Act,  all  contracts,  deeds,  bonds,  agreements,  powers-of-
attorney, grants of legal representation, permissions, approvals, consents or no-objections under any law or otherwise and
other instruments of whatever nature which relate to the said financial asset and which are subsisting or having effect
immediately before the acquisition of financial asset under sub-section (1) and to which the concerned bank or financial
institution is a party or which are in favour of such bank or financial institution shall, after the acquisition of the financial
assets, be of as full force and effect against or in favour of the asset reconstruction company, as the case may be, and may
be enforced or acted upon as fully and effectually as if, in the place of the said bank or financial institution, asset
reconstruction company, as the case may be, had been a party thereto or as if they had been issued in favour of asset
reconstruction company, as the case may be.
(4) If, on the date of acquisition of financial asset under sub-section (1), any suit, appeal or other proceeding of
whatever nature relating to the said financial asset is pending by or against the bank or financial institution, save as
provided in the third proviso to sub-section (1) of Section 15 of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act,
1985 (1 of 1986) the same shall not abate, or be discontinued or be, in any way, prejudicially affected by reason of the
acquisition of financial asset by the asset reconstruction company, as the case may be, but the suit, appeal or other
proceeding may be continued, prosecuted and enforced by or against the asset reconstruction company, as the case may
be.
(5) On acquisition of financial assets under sub-section (1), the asset reconstruction company, may with the
consent of the originator, file an application before the Debts Recovery Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal or any court or
other Authority for the purpose of substitution of its name in any pending suit, appeal or other proceedings and on receipt
of such application, such Debts Recovery Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal or court or Authority shall pass orders for
the substitution of the asset reconstruction company in such pending suit, appeal or other proceedings.

## Page 120

12. What appears on a bare reading is that Section 5 permits an ARC21 to
acquire the financial assets of a bank/financial institution. In terms of
sub-section (1), inter alia, it could be by entering into an agreement for
transfer, on such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between
them. Sub-section (2), which serves as the foundation for sub-section (4),
provides  for  substantive  vesting  of  rights.  By  a  deeming  fiction,  on
acquisition  of  the  financial  assets  by  transfer,  an  ARC  becomes  the
lender  and  all  rights  of  the  bank/financial  institution  vest in  it.  Sub-
section (3) ordains that all contracts, deeds, bonds, agreements, etc.
relating to the asset continue to remain in force in favour of the ARC.
While sub-section (4) is the law providing for procedural continuity, sub-
section (5) governs the procedural aspect for the tribunals, courts and
other authority to abide by when approached by an ARC with a request
for  substitution.  Such  substitution,  however,  is  subject  to  the
requirement thereunder that the application be made with the consent of
the originator.
13. To summarise, the scheme of Section 5 is that on acquisition of the
financial assets, the ARC is deemed to be the lender and as a sequel
thereto, all rights, title and interest of the bank/financial institution vest
in  the  ARC.  The  ARC  can,  subject  to  fulfilment  of  the  statutory
requirements,  continue  pending  proceedings  instituted  by  the
bank/financial institution, as if it were the original secured creditor. By
virtue of sub-sections (4) and (5), having stepped into the shoes of the
original secured creditor, the ARC is entitled to pursue the remedies
21 asset reconstruction company
6

## Page 121

available  to  the  original  secured  creditor  in  relation  to  the  financial
assets so acquired. The right to continue proceedings would, however,
be subject to compliance with the requirements of the statute governing
that particular proceeding or remedy.
14. Whether, sub-sections (4) and (5) of Section 5, authorise the ARC to seek
substitution  in  a  pending  complaint  under  Section  138,  N.I.  Act
necessarily  has  to  be  answered  by  meaningfully  construing  the
expression  “other proceeding of whatever nature relating to the said
financial asset is pending by or against the bank or financial institution”
in sub-section (4) and “for the purpose of substitution of its name in any
pending suit, appeal or other proceedings” in sub-section (5).
15. In our considered opinion, the principle of ejusdem generis would have
no application whilst interpreting either sub-section (4) or sub-section
(5). Sub-section (4) has an in-built exception clause. When expressly
referring  to  the  SICA22,  Parliament  in  its  wisdom  provided  that  if  a
reference  to  the  BIFR23 abates  under  SICA,  then  sub-section  (4)  of
Section 5 will not save it. However, this exception does not apply to all
proceedings; it applies to only one proceeding, i.e., under the SICA. The
words  “suit, appeal or other proceeding” are not qualified as ‘civil’ or
‘recovery’  proceedings;  on  the  contrary,  the  expression  “other
proceeding  of  whatever  nature” is  deliberately  unqualified.  It  takes
colour from the engrafted exception – the third proviso to Section 15(1),
SICA – which relates to a proceeding before the BIFR, a proceeding that is
22 Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985
23 Board for Financial and Industrial Reconstruction
7

## Page 122

neither a suit nor an appeal. The exception, thus, shows that  “other
proceeding” cannot be read ejusdem generis with the words “suit” and
“appeal” and is intended to travel beyond suits and appeals, which are
generally associated with civil proceedings, and to include proceedings
of a different nature, including a complaint under Section 138, N.I. Act
relating to a financial asset. This interpretation is also consistent with the
legislative object underlying Section 5, which is to facilitate acquisition of
financial  assets  and  ensure  continuity  of  the  rights  and  remedies
attached thereto. The fact that a proceeding under Section 138 of the
N.I.  Act  is  criminal  in  form  would  not,  by  itself,  exclude  it  from  the
expression  “other  proceeding  of  whatever  nature”,  provided  that  it
relates to the financial asset acquired by the ARC and was pending by or
against the bank or financial institution on the date of such acquisition.
Sub-section  (4)  of  Section  5,  for  all  intents  and  purposes,  having
provided for a continuity and the words “other proceeding of whatever
nature” used by Parliament being very wide, the same must be allowed
to operate in its full amplitude. Such width is intentional to ensure that
no proceeding relating to the financial asset is lost for want of a party to
prosecute it.
16. However,  we  add  a  caveat  here.  While  a  pending  complaint  under
Section 138, N.I. Act does not abate on assignment to an ARC of the
financial asset/debt under sub-section (1) of Section 5 of the SARFAESI
Act, such assignment does not, per se, make the ARC the payee or the
holder in due course. The ARC, to continue proceedings, must still prove
that  (i)  the  cheque,  since  dishonoured,  itself  was  transferred  and
8

## Page 123

delivered  to  it  along  with  the  financial  asset  and  not  merely  the
underlying debt; (ii) there has been an endorsement/assignment in its
favour sufficient to constitute it as a holder in due course under Sections
8 and 9 of the N.I. Act; (iii) the ingredients of Section 138 of the N.I. Act
are satisfied; and (iv) there is no attempt to improve upon the case of
the original complainant/secured creditor. Therefore, while permitting a
substitution, the ARC has to be put to strict proof that the ARC is the
“holder  in  due  course”.  Such  question(s)  of  fact  must  obviously  be
decided on the basis of evidence led at the trial.
17. We, therefore, dismiss the special leave petition. 
18. However, it is clarified that apart from the points decided by the trial
magistrate  while  granting  the  prayer  for  substitution  of  the  first
respondent, since confirmed by the Sessions Court and ultimately by the
High  Court  in  the  impugned  judgment,  all  other  contentions  of  the
accused/petitioners,  available  in  law,  are  kept  open  for  being  urged
before the trial magistrate for being decided in accordance with law.
19. Connected applications, if any, shall stand disposed of.

disclose  the  active  role  played  by  the

filed.

Leave granted.
Being aggrieved by the order dated 01.05.2025
passed by the learned single Judge of the High Court
of  Judicature  for  Rajasthan  at  Jodhpur  in  S.B.
Criminal Misc (Pet.) No.3338 of 2025, the appellant,
who is the husband of the second respondent, has
preferred this appeal.
Learned  counsel  for  the  respective  parties
submitted that during the pendency of this appeal the
parties were referred to the Supreme Court Mediation
Centre. The parties have arrived at a settlement
agreement  dated  19.09.2026  under  which  they  have
1

## Page 159

decided to part ways and seek dissolution of their
marriage by a decree of divorce by mutual consent. 
  Learned  counsel  for  the  respective  parties
submitted that the terms of the settlement agreement
state  that  the  parties  would  not  prosecute  the
respective cases they have filed against each other
and therefore the said proceedings may be quashed.
The parties have also filed a joint application under
Article 142 of the Constitution of India seeking
dissolution of their marriage by a decree of divorce
by mutual consent invoking Section 13B of the Hindu
Marriage  Act,  1955.  They  submitted  that  the
settlement agreement dated 19.09.2026 as well as the
Joint Application may be taken on record and relief
may be granted to the parties and consequently, this
appeal may be disposed of.
The parties are present before this Court. They
have been identified by their respective counsel.
When  queried,  they  stated  that  they  have  indeed
arrived at a settlement of their disputes; that they
do not wish to continue their marital life; that they
would wish to seek dissolution of their marriage by a
2

## Page 160

decree of divorce by mutual consent and they would
abide  by  the  terms  of  settlement.  In  the
circumstances,  this  Court  may  pass  orders
accordingly. 
In the above backdrop, we have taken on record
the settlement agreement dated 19.09.2026 and the
joint application filed under Article 142 of the
Constitution of India. We have perused the same. We
find that there are no specific terms of settlement
arrived at as such between the parties. However,
learned counsel for the respective parties submitted
that the following cases may be quashed and the Joint
Application  filed  under  Article  142  of  the
Constitution may be ordered.
“i.  Petition  bearing  no.  Family  Main
Case/64/2025 titled as Pooja vs Ashish under
Section 13(1) (1A) of the Hindu Marriage Act for
dissolution of marriage, which is pending before
Family Court, Nohar, District- Hanumangarh.
ii.  Petition  bearing  no.  Family  Main
Case/248/2026 titled as Ashish vs Pooja under
Section  9  of  the  Hindu  Marriage  Act  for
restitution of conjugal rights, pending before
Family Court, Nohar, District- Hanumangarh.
Iii. Criminal Case bearing registration number
Cr. Reg. Case/416/2026 arising out of FIR No.
123/2025 registered at Police Station- Nohar,
District-  Hanumangarh,  Rajasthan  for  the
offences punishable under Sections 85, 316(2),
3

## Page 161

115(2),  352,  3(5),  61(2)  and  318(4)  of  the
Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita (BNS) registered at the
instance of the Second Party against the First
Party and his family members, which is pending
before ACJM, Nohar, District- Hanumangarh.”
We have perused the Joint Application under
Article 142 of the Constitution. The parties seek
dissolution of their marriage by decree of divorce by
mutual  consent.  Having  perused  the  terms  of  the
Settlement Agreement, we find that there is no legal
impediment in accepting the same.
Consequently,  we  accept  the  terms  of  the
settlement. The same shall be read as part and parcel
of this order. 
Joint Application (IA NO.333069 of 2026) filed
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India also
stands  allowed.  The  marriage  between  the  parties
solemnised  on  18.02.2022  at  Elienabad,  District
Sirsa, Haryana is dissolved by a decree of divorce by
mutual consent.
The Registry is directed to draw up a decree in
the aforesaid terms.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 291/2011 
 
 
 
STATE OF U.P. & ORS       APPELLANT(S) 
 
VERSUS 
 
GRAND SLAM FITNESS(P) LTD.            RESPONDENT(S) 
 
WITH 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 293/2011 
 
 
ORDER 
 
 
1. Heard Mr. Bhakti Vardhan Singh and                       
Ms. Charanya Lakshmikumaran, learned counsel for the 
parties. 
2. The respondents in Civil Misc. Writ Petition 
No. 534/2009 and Civil Misc. Writ Petition No. 
361/2009 are the appellants. 
3. The Writ Petitioners are private limited 
companies incorporated under the provisions of the 
Companies Act, 1956. They are primarily engaged in 
the sale of physical exercise and fitness equipment, 
such as the Cross Elliptical Trainer, Manual 
Treadmill, Motorized Treadmill, Rowers Exercise 
Bikes, Strength Equipment, etc. The petitioners are 
registered dealers under the U.P. Value Added Tax 
Act, 2008. The companies have filed a Writ of 

## Page 166

2 
 
Certiorari against the order dated 18.09.2008 passed 
by the second appellant and the order dated 
26.11.2008 passed by the third appellant in the Civil 
Appeals. The subject-matter relates to the period 
from April, 2008 to July, 2008. 
4. Through the order dated 31.10.2008, the 
Revenue called upon the dealers to pay tax @ 12.5% 
under the Act on the sports equipment dealt with by 
the dealers. Here, we use the expression equipment 
inasmuch as the controversy between the Revenue and 
the dealers centres around the nature, name, and code 
entry to which it belongs, and whether the equipment 
dealt with by the dealers falls within the exemption 
granted vide notification dated 09.04.2008. 
5. To appreciate the controversy, the following 
few lines are adverted to: 
5.1 The dealers claim that the equipment falls 
under Commodity Code Entry No. 60 under Section 70 
of the Act under which the goods have been 
classified. The exemption notification dated 
09.04.2008 reads as under: 
“51. Wooden Toys, Lac + Shellac, 
including Paseva Mulamma, Button, Leo and 
Kiri, Sports Goods excluding Apparels, 
and sports Footwear, stop clock. 
A true typed copy of the Notification No. 
1021 dated 9/4 2008 is annexed herewith 
and marked as ANNEXURE P-2 to this SLP.” 

## Page 167

3 
 
 
6. Therefore, since the equipment dealt with by 
the dealer squarely falls within the definition of 
‘Sports Goods’, first, the levy and imposition of 
tax on exempted goods is impermissible, and second, 
levying tax @ 12.5%, which treats it as unclassified 
goods, is illegal. Hence, prayed for setting aside 
the demand. 
7. The case of Revenue is that the notification 
dated 09.04.2008 employs broad expressions, and from 
the perspective of the revenue, the subsequent 
notification issued would make it clear that, through 
the notification dated 09.04.2008, the revenue did 
not treat the equipment dealt with by the dealer as 
sports goods. Therefore, for the subsequent periods, 
the levy is tenable. 
8. The above controversy has been considered by 
the High Court in the impugned judgment. The High 
Court first referred to Section 70 of the Act and 
the commodity code assigned by the revenue. It is 
not in dispute that Entry No. 60 under the commodity 
codes deals with “sports Goods, Games and Toys”. 
Therefore, the High Court is of the view that there 
is no good or valid reason to exclude the equipment 
dealt with by the dealer from the meaning of sports 
goods. Consequently, the High Court has set aside 

## Page 168

4 
 
the impugned notice. 
9. The learned counsel appearing for the State 
argues that the High Court ought to have given 
meaning to the expression ‘sports goods’ in relation 
to the notification dated 09.04.2008. Under such an 
understanding, it cannot be said that the equipment 
dealt with by the dealer can be treated as sports 
goods. Therefore, it is argued that the assessments 
dated 18.09.2008 and 26.11.2008 were validly issued 
and that the High Court ought not to have interfered 
with them. 
10. Advocate Charanya Lakshmikumaran, appearing 
for the dealer, contends that the commodity entry is 
general but includes the equipment dealt with by the 
dealer. The reason assigned by the revenue for 
imposing tax @ 12.5% is completely illegal and 
unsustainable. Once the power of the revenue under 
Section 70 of the Act is exercised and the commodity 
code is prepared, denying the benefit of the 
exemption issued through notification dated 
09.04.2008 is illegal. The reasoning of the High 
Court is brief but tenable, and she prays for 
dismissal of the Civil Appeal. 
11. We have taken note of the submissions and 
perused the entries. 
13. Let us first begin with Entry No. 60 (supra), 

## Page 169

5 
 
which includes sports goods, games and toys. Let us 
juxtapose Entry No. 51 in Schedule-I, amended through 
the notification dated 09.04.2008. The conclusion is 
that the exemption clearly deals with sports goods. 
We have to juxtapose the exemption in the 
notification dated 09.04.2008 with Commodity Code 
No. 60, which deals with sports goods, games and 
toys. A simple juxtaposition of both the entries 
would make it clear that the equipment being dealt 
with by the dealers can be classified as sports 
goods. The impugned order is correct and has applied 
the correct provision of law and the exemption entry. 
14. We see no reason to interfere with the 
impugned order(s). 
15. The Civil Appeals are, accordingly, 
dismissed. 
16. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand 
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 7038 OF 2025
BSE LTD. ..... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
SPICE ENERGY PVT. LTD. & ANR. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. By order dated 26.04.2023, the Review Committee of the Bombay
Stock Exchange Limited1 rejected the request made by Spice
Energy Pvt. Ltd.2, respondent No. 1 herein, for de-freezing of
its  demat  account  effected  under  the  communication  dated
14.01.2023 of the Surveillance Cell of the National Securities
Depository Limited. Aggrieved thereby, SEPL approached the
Securities Appellate Tribunal3 at Mumbai by way of Appeal No.
569/2023.  The said appeal was allowed on 30.04.2025 with costs
of 1,00,000/- (Rupees one lakh only). Thereby, the order dated₹
26.04.2023 passed by the Review Committee of the BSE was
quashed and it was directed to refund the entire amount
realized from SEPL with respect to the outstanding dues of the
Annual Listing Fees (AFL) in respect of M/s. Cals Refineries
Limited, along with interest, and also de-freeze its demat
account immediately.
2. By order dated 30.05.2025 passed in the present appeal, this
1  “BSE”, for short
2  “SEPL”, for short
3  “SAT”, for short
C.A. No. 7038/2025     1

## Page 186

Court stayed the impugned order dated 30.04.2025 passed by the
SAT.
3. The aforestated order dated 30.04.2025 reflects that the SAT
was of the opinion that, as Cals Refineries Limited was
subjected to Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under the
provisions of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 20164, upon
the admission on 17.10.2017 of a company petition filed against
it under Section 9 thereof, the matter was amenable to disposal
on a short point, that is, the moratorium that would operate
under Section 14 of the IBC against the corporate debtor.
Applying Section 238 of the IBC, which states to the effect
that  the  provisions  of  the  IBC  shall  have  effect
notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in
any other law, the SAT opined that recovery of the outstanding
ALF dues of the corporate debtor could not be effected against
an erstwhile promoter of the corporate debtor.  The argument of
the BSE that the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC would
apply only to the corporate debtor and not to its promoters,
was rejected on the ground that such an interpretation would
defeat the very purpose of the IBC.
4. The aforestated construction of Section 14 of the IBC by the
SAT militates against the very language used therein.  The
moratorium that operates under that provision would only be in
the context of the corporate debtor and not its promoters or
directors. The SAT merely relied upon this provision and
4  “IBC”, for short
C.A. No. 7038/2025     2

## Page 187

thereby applied Section 238 of the IBC. It is, therefore,
manifest  that  the  SAT  disposed  of  the  matter  without
considering and applying its mind to the other issues that had
been raised in the appeal by SEPL.  
5. We may note that, in the context of the liability sought to be
pinned upon the SEPL, the interpretation and application of the
Circulars issued by the Securities and Exchange Board of India,
respondent No.2 herein, under the Securities and Exchange Board
of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements)
Regulations, 2015, also arose for consideration. Though the
validity  of  the  Circulars  and  the  Regulations  was  never
subjected to challenge by SEPL, the construction thereof and
their application was very much within the ken of the enquiry
by the SAT in the appeal. However, the SAT failed to undertake
this exercise as it chose to dispose of the appeal by applying
Section 14 of the IBC to SEPL also. The issue raised as to its
status vis-a-vis the corporate debtor was also not considered,
despite a specific ground having been raised in the appeal.
6. In the light of the cursory disposal of the appeal by the SAT
without going into the questions that arose therein, be it on
facts or in law, we are constrained to set aside the impugned
order dated 30.04.2025 and remand the matter to the SAT for
consideration afresh on merits and in accordance with law.
7. We  may  note  that,  pursuant  to  the  interim  order  dated
10.02.2026 passed by this Court in I.A. No. 203072/2025, the
earlier interim order dated 30.05.2025 stood modified to the
C.A. No. 7038/2025     3

## Page 188

extent of permitting the de-freezing of the demat account of
SEPL upon deposit of a sum of 58,04,505/- (Rupees fifty eight₹
lakhs four thousand five hundred five only) with the BSE,
without prejudice and under protest.  We are informed that
acting upon the aforestated order, SEPL paid the said sum of
money to BSE without prejudice and under protest.  As we are
are now remitting the matter to the SAT for consideration
afresh, such payment shall abide by the result of the appeal
after such consideration by the SAT. We may make it clear that
all issues have been left open for consideration by the SAT,
including the entitlement of SEPL to claim refund along with
interest, if any, in the event it succeeds in the appeal.
8. The appeal is disposed of, accordingly.  
Parties shall bear their own costs.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard Mr. Yatin Oza, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
applicant in Miscellaneous Application No. 3299 of 2026; Mr. Shyam
Divan, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondent-HDFC
Bank  Limited,  the  original  respondent  in  the  Special  Leave
Petition; and Mr. Nachiketa Joshi, learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the Bankruptcy Trustee, who was the petitioner in the original
Special Leave Petition.
2. The present Miscellaneous Application has been filed seeking
clarification of the order dated 01.10.2026 to the effect that the
said order does not preclude the applicant from placing his case
before the learned Mediator.
3. Further, it is prayed that a clarification be issued to the
effect that the order dated 01.10.2026 does not preclude the
continuation of Commercial Suit No. 157 of 2016.
4. The Special Leave Petition itself arose under the following
circumstances:-
In a pending suit filed by the applicant/Respondent no.2, Mr.
Bhupendra Jivrajbhai Surani, against the HDFC Bank, the Bankruptcy
Trustee, Mr. Alan Chung Wah Tang, sought to be impleaded as a
plaintiff on the ground that the plaintiff had been declared
bankrupt and the assets, including the shares in question, had
vested in the Bankruptcy Trustee.
We are not concerned with the other details of the suit for

## Page 199

3
the purpose of the present proceedings.
The HDFC Bank, which is the defendant in the suit, filed
Notice of Motion No. 763 of 2019 along with Interim Application No.
4412 of 2026, seeking to restrain the Bankruptcy Trustee from
proceeding with the proceedings in Action No. 473 of 2026 pending
before the High Court of the Hong Kong, Special Administrative
Region(SAR).
On 24.08.2026, the learned Single Judge of the High Court
directed  that  the  Bankruptcy  Trustee  and  the  authorized
representative Mr. Vinod Kaushik, be restrained from proceeding
with the Hong Kong Proceedings viz., Action No. 473 of 2026 before
the High Court of Hong Kong(SAR). 
Aggrieved  by  the  order  dated  24.08.2026,  the  Bankruptcy
Trustee filed the Special Leave Petition(C)No.33989 of 2026 before
this Court, contending that an order in the nature of an anti-suit
injunction ought not to have been passed at the behest of HDFC Bank
in the circumstances of the case.
When that Special Leave Petition came up for hearing on
01.10.2026, the only issue under consideration was whether the
order dated 24.08.2026 passed by the learned Single Judge of the
High Court in I.A.No.4412 of 2026 in Notice of Motion No. 763 of
2019 in Commercial Suit No. 157 of 2016, was justified or not.
The parties, who were at daggers drawn before us, were the
Bankruptcy Trustee on the one hand and the HDFC bank on the other.
After hearing the parties for some time, we passed the
following order and disposed of the Special Leave Petition on
01.10.2026:-

## Page 200

4
“1. Heard Mr. Santosh Paul, learned Senior Counsel for
the petitioners and Mr. Shyam Divan, learned Senior
Counsel appearing on caveat for contesting respondent-
HDFC Bank Limited. 
2. Having heard the submissions made by the learned
Senior Counsel for the parties, we are of the opinion,
that the contesting parties, namely, the petitioner(s)
and  HDFC  Bank  Limited,  should  sit  together  and
mediate.
3. Parties have favourably responded to the suggestion
of  the  Court  that  an  attempt  for  an  amicable
resolution to the dispute be explored through the
process of mediation.
4. We request to Hon’ble Justice Abhay S. Oka, Former
Judge of this Court to act as a Mediator in this
matter with the consent of both the parties. The
learned Mediator make an attempt to amicably resolved
the matter.
5. Parties to get in touch with the learned Mediator
and  appear  on  a  date  convenient  to  the  learned
Mediator.
6. The fees and other terms payable to the learned
Mediator shall be fixed in consultation with the
parties.
7. We are conscious that the proceedings are pending
before the High Court of Judicature at Bombay and we
notice that some applications are slated for hearing
on 05.10.2026 before the High Court.
8. The learned Mediator may, as and when the report is
ready, forwarded the same to the High Court in the
pending proceedings. The interim arrangement made by
the High Court shall continue till the mediation
proceedings conclude.
9. Learned counsel for the petitioner(s) submits that
the High Court proceeding may be stayed.
10. The pendency of mediation may be brought to the
notice of the High Court.
11. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of in the
above terms.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.”
5. As is clear from the order passed by this Court on 01.10.2026,
we referred the matter to mediation before Hon’ble Mr. Justice

## Page 201

5
Abhay S.Oka, Former Judge of this Court, to mediate the dispute
between the Bankruptcy Trustee and the HDFC Bank.
6. The present application has been filed by the plaintiff
contending that he was not only the plaintiff in the suit but was
also arrayed as respondent no.2 in the Special Leave Petition filed
by the Bankruptcy Trustee and that he ought to have been heard
before passing the order.
7. Mr. Yatin Oza, learned Senior Counsel, submits that notice was
not issued to the respondent no.2 in the Special Leave Petition and
the matter was disposed of by referring the Bankruptcy Trustee and
the HDFC Bank to mediation.
8. On the other hand, Mr. Shyam Divan, learned Senior Counsel,
contends  that  the  applicant  has  no  locus  to  maintain  the
Miscellaneous Application or to participate in the mediation.
9. The dispute between the Bankruptcy Trustee and the HDFC Bank
was about the claim of HDFC Bank against the applicant herein, who
stood as a guarantor for a loan, to secure which the shares had
been pledged.
10. Mr. Divan, learned Senior Counsel, vehemently opposed the
participation of the applicant in the mediation.
11. Mr. Nachiketa Joshi, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
Bankruptcy Trustee, submitted that once the Trustee had been
appointed, the applicant had no locus standi in the suit.
12. We are not concerned with any of the above disputes inter se
between the parties.
13. The narrow issue before us in the Special Leave Petition was
about the correctness of the order dated 24.08.2026 passed by the

## Page 202

6
High Court of Judicature at Bombay. It was in those circumstances
that  HDFC  Bank  and  the  Bankruptcy  Trustee  were  referred  to
mediation.
14. However, considering that the applicant, who is the plaintiff
in the suit and was respondent no.2 in the Special Leave Petition,
is desirous of participating in the mediation, we direct that the
applicant shall have the liberty to participate in the mediation
and place his case before the learned mediator.
15. Needless to say, this will not preclude the Bankruptcy Trustee
and the HDFC Bank from entering into any agreement, if so advised.
16. Needless to further observe, the applicant is always at
liberty to initiate such action or continue such proceedings, if
maintainable in law, to secure his rights, if any. 
17. We also notice that that the mediation has made significant
progress. The learned mediator has already concluded two sittings.
18. Our order dated 01.10.2026 does not, in any manner, adjudicate
on the existence or otherwise of any rights of the applicant
herein.
19. Our  order  also  does  not  discontinue  the  suit  bearing
Commercial  Suit  No.  157  of  2016.   Hence,  prayer  B  in  the
application is not tenable.
20. With  the  above  observations,  the  present  Miscellaneous
Application stands disposed of.
21. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
(VARSHA MENDIRATTA)                         (AKSHAY KUMAR BHORIA)

ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant;
learned counsel for Respondent No.1-State of Madhya
Pradesh;  and  learned  counsel  for  Respondent  No.2-
informant.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 17.07.2026
passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Gwalior
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
prayer for anticipatory bail of the appellant.
4. Appellant has been named as an accused in FIR
No.238/2026 registered at Police Station- Bahodapur,
District- Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh under Section 108 of
the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for short, ‘BNS’).
1

## Page 204

5. Prosecution case, in brief, is that Mayank Goyal
had consumed poisonous substance and during the course
of  treatment,  passed  away  on  21.05.2026.  As  per
statement of the father of the deceased Mukesh Goyal,
he had given Rs.12,00,000/- to his son Mayank Goyal and
the appellant for being invested in property business.
When  his  daughter’s  wedding  was  approaching,  P.W.1
asked Mayank to bring back his Rs.12,00,000/-. However,
when Mayank approached the appellant, he refused to
return back the money. When appellant categorically
refused to return back the money on 20.05.2026, Mayank
Goyal  consumed  poison  which  led  to  his  death  on
21.05.2026.
6. This Court, by order dated 03.08.2026, had issued
notice and granted interim protection to the appellant
subject  to  the  appellant  co-operating  with  the
investigation, pursuant to which the respondents have
filed counter affidavits which we have perused.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that
appellant is a Dentist by profession. Residence of the
deceased is in the neighbourhood of his clinic. He
submits that though there were financial transactions
between the appellant and the deceased, those were not
related  to  any  property  business.  He  denies  the
accusation  that  because  of  the  abetment  by  the
2

## Page 205

appellant,  deceased  committed  suicide.  Further
submission of learned counsel for the appellant is that
pursuant  to  the  interim  protection  granted  by
this  Court,  appellant  has  co-operated  with  the
investigation.
8. Per contra, learned counsel for Respondent No.1-
State of Madhya Pradesh has referred to the counter
affidavit and vehemently argued that it is a case for
custodial  interrogation  of  the  appellant.  He  has
referred to the statement made by the father of the
deceased under Section 194 of the Bharatiya Nagarik
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (for short, ‘BNSS’) where he
categorically stated that because of the appellant not
returning  Rs.12,00,000/-  for  the  wedding  of  his
daughter,  deceased  committed  suicide  by  consuming
poison  as  he  was  being  mentally  and  physically
tortured. He has also referred to another statement
made by one Virender Singh Sengar before the police, on
the basis of which he submits that the said Virender
Singh Sengar had given three cheques to the appellant
and  to  the  deceased,  totalling  Rs.42,00,000/-  for
investing in property business. However, when he sought
return of the money, appellant refused to return back
the same. He submits that the deceased was under mental
stress on account of the conduct of the appellant which
3

## Page 206

is the proximate reason for him committing suicide.
9. Similar is the stand taken by learned counsel for
Respondent No.2-informant. He submits that from the
materials on record gathered thus, it is evident that
appellant had a definite role to play in abetting
commission of suicide by the deceased. There is need
for  further  investigation  for  which  custodial
interrogation of the appellant is necessary.
10. We have considered the submissions made by learned
counsel for the parties.
11. While there appears to be financial transactions
between the appellant and the deceased, at this stage,
it cannot be said for sure that appellant had abetted
the deceased to commit suicide. There can be various
other angles to the unfortunate death of Mayank Goyal.
We  would  not  like  to  express  any  opinion  on  the
investigation carried out thus far but we are of the
view that in a case of this nature when the appellant
has  co-operated  with  the  investigation,  denial  of
anticipatory bail to the appellant would not be just
and proper.
12. Considering the above, we are of the view that the
interim protection granted by this Court vide order
dated 03.08.2026 should be made absolute.
13. That being the position, we set aside the impugned
4

## Page 207

order dated 17.07.2026 passed by the High Court and
make our order dated 03.08.2026 absolute. However, the
appellant  shall  continue  to  co-operate  with  the
investigation of the case.
14. Consequently, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
15. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

O R D E R
1. The present transfer petition has been filed by the
petitioners (in-laws), aged about 75 years and 65 years
respectively,  seeking  transfer  of  the  maintenance
proceedings  instituted by  the respondent(daughter-in-
law) i.e. Cr. Misc. Case No. 483 of 2024, titled as
“Smt. Hem Prabha vs. Sh. Shiv Kumar Rajpal & Anr.”,
pending  before  the  Family  Court  Judge-3,  District
Udaipur,  Rajasthan  to  the  court  of  competent
jurisdiction at District Purnea, Bihar.
2. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioners submits
that the petitioners are senior citizens suffering from
renal disorders and other age related ailments, and are
unable to travel from Bihar to Udaipur, Rajasthan to
contest the proceedings, whereas the respondent is aged
1

## Page 210

about  35  years  and  can  conveniently  attend  the
proceedings at Bihar.
3. The prayer for transfer has been vehemently opposed
by learned counsel appearing for the respondent.
4. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and
taking into consideration the advanced aged (75 years
and 65 years) and medical condition of the petitioners,
this Court is of the opinion that the maintenance case
deserves to be transferred. 
5. Accordingly,  we  allow  the  transfer  petition  and
direct the transfer of case bearing Cr. Misc. Case No.
483 of 2024, titled as “Smt. Hem Prabha vs. Sh. Shiv
Kumar Rajpal & Anr.”, pending before the Family Court
Judge-3, District Udaipur, Rajasthan to the court of
competent jurisdiction at District Purnea, Bihar.
6. Let the record of the case be transferred without
delay.
7. A copy of this order be sent to the concerned court
for  compliance.  If  video  conferencing  facility  is
available with the transferee Court, the benefit of the
same shall be extended to the parties on such dates when
their physical appearance is not required. It is made
clear that this Court has not expressed any opinion on
2

## Page 211

the merits of the matter.
8. The parties shall appear before the Family Court,
District Purnea, Bihar, on 01.12.2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION (C) NO.82 OF 2026
SIMRANJIT SINGH PETITIONER(S)
                              VERSUS
RAMANPREET SINGH RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This petition under Section 11(6) read with Section
11(12)(a) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
(for short, "the Act") has been filed by the petitioner, a
citizen of New Zealand and holder of an Overseas Citizen of
India  (OCI)  card,  seeking  the  appointment  of  a  Sole
Arbitrator for the adjudication of disputes arising out of
a Settlement Agreement dated 10.02.2025 executed between
the parties.
2. The petitioner, being a foreign national ordinarily
residing outside India, invokes the jurisdiction of this
Court  as  the  dispute  constitutes  an  "International
Commercial Arbitration" within the meaning of Section 2(1)
(f)(i) of the Act. Clause 2.8 of the Settlement Agreement
provides for the resolution of disputes through binding
1

## Page 259

arbitration under the Act, with the seat of arbitration in
India and governed by Indian law.
3. A perusal of the record reveals that the petitioner
duly invoked the arbitration clause by serving a legal
notice dated 20.09.2025 upon the respondent, calling upon
him to amicably resolve the disputes within 15 days in
terms of Clause 2.8. The respondent sent a reply dated
04.10.2025 denying the claims without consenting to an
amicable resolution or the appointment of an arbitrator.
4. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and upon
perusing the material on record, we are satisfied that a
valid arbitration agreement exists between the parties and
that arbitrable disputes have arisen thereunder.
5. Accordingly, we allow the present petition and appoint
Mr. Sanjeev Sharma, Senior Advocate (Mobile No.9888017329),
as the Sole Arbitrator to adjudicate the disputes and
differences  between  the  parties  arising  out  of  the
Settlement  Agreement  dated  10.02.2025.  The  seat  of
arbitration shall be at Chandigarh.
6. The learned Sole Arbitrator shall be at liberty to fix
his fees in consultation with the parties.
7. All rights and contentions of the parties, including
the right to file counter-claim, if any, are kept open to
be decided by the learned Sole Arbitrator in accordance
with law.
2

disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION (C) NO.49 OF 2026
INDIES PHARMA JAMAICA LIMITED PETITIONER(S)
                              VERSUS
ZYDUS LIFESCIENCES LIMITED 
(FORMERLY CADILLA HEALTHCARE LIMITED)
RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This petition under Section 11(6) read with Section
11(12)(a) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (for
short,  "the  Act"),  seeks  the  appointment  of  a  Sole
Arbitrator to adjudicate the disputes arising between the
parties out of the Contract Manufacturing Agreement dated
20.05.2021 (for short, "CMA") read with the Letter of Intent
dated 14.12.2020 (for short, "LOI").
2. Briefly stated, the Petitioner, Indies Pharma Jamaica
Limited, is a pharmaceutical company incorporated under the
laws of Jamaica, while the Respondent, Zydus Lifesciences
Limited (formerly Cadilla Healthcare Limited), is a company
incorporated under the laws of India. The parties entered
into the aforesaid LOI and CMA for the technology transfer
documents, contract manufacturing, and supply of a generic
version of the drug 'Nelarabine' for commercialization in
the United States of America. Article 18(a) of the CMA
contains  the  dispute  resolution  clause,  providing  for
arbitration  in  accordance  with  the  provisions  of  the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, with the seat/venue
1

## Page 263

at Ahmedabad, India.
3. Disputes arose between the parties regarding alleged
delays  in  completing  requisite  scientific  studies  and
deliverables for filing the Abbreviated New Drug Application
(ANDA) before the USFDA. After issuing a Legal Notice dated
18.11.2024 seeking amicable settlement under Article 18(a)
of the CMA, to which the Respondent replied on 09.12.2024
declining settlement  discussions, the  Petitioner invoked
arbitration vide Notice dated 02.04.2025 under Section 21 of
the Act and proposed the appointment of a Sole Arbitrator.
The Respondent, vide reply dated 02.05.2025, disputed the
existence of an arbitrable dispute and declined to consent
to the appointment. Hence, the present petition.
4. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and
perused the material placed on record.
5. Having regard to the limited scope of inquiry under
Section 11 of the Act and the fact that the existence of the
arbitration agreement is not in dispute, we deem it just and
proper  to  allow  the  present  petition.  All  preliminary
objections and contentions of the parties, including the
issue of limitation, which is a mixed question of fact and
law,  are  kept  open  to  be  adjudicated  by  the  learned
Arbitrator. 
6. Accordingly, we appoint Hon’ble Mr. Justice Rashmin M.
Chhaya, Former Chief Justice of Gauhati High Court, as the
Sole Arbitrator to adjudicate the disputes and differences
between the parties arising out of and in connection with
the aforesaid agreements.
7. The seat and venue of the arbitration, in accordance
with Article 18(a) of the CMA, shall be Ahmedabad, India.
8. The learned Sole Arbitrator shall be at liberty to fix
his fees in consultation with the parties.
2

terms.
10. Pending interlocutory applications, if any, also stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CIVIL) NO. 11318 OF 2024)
SATYANARAYAN MAHAKUD APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
RAJ KUMAR SARAIWALA & ANR. RESPONDENT(S)
W I T H
CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CIVIL) NO. 7024 OF 2025)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (“Tribunal”) had directed
the insurance company to pay a compensation of 7,29,161/- with 6%₹
interest from 18.08.2015. The incident occurred on 28.04.2015 when
the appellant(s) had suffered injury while riding a motorcycle
owing to rash and negligent driving of a pickup van bearing
registration number OR-11-E-3229. The Tribunal order came to be
challenged both by the appellant(s) as well as the insurance
company. The High Court observed that the appellant had suffered
temporary disability up to 50% till the year 2022, and accordingly
applied  multiplier  7  instead  of  14,  thereby  reducing  the
compensation  to  5,61,161/-.  We  have  examined  the  disability₹
certificate and we are in agreement with the Tribunal that though
the disability certificate shows that the disability was up to 50%
till 2022, it cannot be said that such disability would not impair
the earning potential of the appellant(s) beyond such date.  Given
1

## Page 271

these circumstances, we hold the High Court had erred in reducing
the compensation as aforesaid.  However, we are not inclined to
enhance the compensation awarded by the Tribunal.  
3. Accordingly, we set aside the order(s) of the High Court and
restore the order of the Tribunal. The appeals are allowed to such
extent.
             
..........................J.
       (JOYMALYA BAGCHI)
..........................J.
       (V. MOHANA)

pendency of the appeal before the High Court.
4. Appellant has been convicted by the Special Court
under Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for
short, ‘IPC’) and under Sections 15 and 18 of the Narcotic
Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (for short,
‘NDPS Act’) in NDPS Case No.06 of 2022. Consequent upon

Imprisonment (for short, ‘R.I.’) for a period of 10 years

## Page 283

and to pay a fine of Rs.1,00,000/-, with a default
stipulation.
5. Appellant has assailed his conviction and sentence
before the High Court in Criminal Appeal (D.B.) No.386 of
2024, which is pending. Appellant also filed I.A. No.9932
of 2025 for suspending the sentence and to release him on
bail during pendency of the appeal.
6. By the impugned order dated 18.09.2025, the High
Court declined to suspend the sentence and dismissed the
interlocutory application of the appellant.
7. This  Court  had  issued  notice  vide  order  dated
08.06.2026,  pursuant  to  which  respondent-State  of
Jharkhand has filed counter affidavit.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that he has
already undergone incarceration for more than three years.
The  seized  contraband  is  less  than  the  commercial
quantity, though it is a large quantity. He further
submits that the other convict Md. Suhel @ Md. Suhail has
been granted bail by the High Court. Appellant has also
been acquitted in NDPS Case No.07 of 2018. He submits that
appellant has a good case on merit and is hopeful of
success in the criminal appeal before the High Court.
9. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent-State
of Jharkhand submits that the sentence undergone by the
appellant is less than half of the total sentence imposed
on him. The seizure pertains to 27 kgs of poppy husk,
which is a large quantity and he has been found guilty by

the Trial Court. Therefore, the sentence imposed by the
Trial Court may not be suspended.

due consideration, we are of the view that it may not be
possible for the High Court to hear the appeal filed by
the appellant in the near future, which is of the year
2024.  In  the  meanwhile,  the  appellant  has  already
undergone more than 03 years of incarceration.
11. That being the position, we are inclined to suspend

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Being aggrieved by the order dated 25.09.2025 passed by the
High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur in Misc. Criminal Case
No.17123 of 2023, the petitioners are before this Court by the
present Special Leave Petition viz.,SLP (Crl.)NO(S).18316 of 2024.
2. The wife of the petitioners in SLP (Crl.) No(s).18316 of 2024
also preferred another petition viz., SLP (Crl.) No.3478 of 2026
being aggrieved by the order dated 15.07.2025 passed by the High
Court of Mahdya Pradesh at Indore in Writ Petition No.35931 of 2024
and therefore, this Court is deciding both the matters by this
common order.
3. The facts of the case reveal that being aggrieved by the
registration of the FIR viz., FIR No.33 of 2023 dated 27.01.2023
against the petitioner and his father, the petitioners preferred a
petition under Section 482 CRPC before the High Court of Madhya
Pradesh Bench at Jabalpur. The first two paragraphs of the order
passed by the High Court categorically mention that the petitioners
have approached the High Court seeking quashment of FIR registered
at Police Station Kymore, District Katni for offences punishable
under Sections 498-A and 506 of IPC and Section 3 and 4 of the
Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. The High Court  vide  impugned order
dated 25.09.2024 dismissed the quash petition and the present
Special Leave Petition arising out of the aforesaid order.
4. The petitioners whose petition under Section 482 CRPC was
2

## Page 288

dismissed vide impugned order by the Principal Seat of the High
Court at Jabalpur suppressing the aforesaid fact filed another
petition under Section 482 CrPC (422 of the Bharatiya Nagarik
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023) for quashment of the very same FIR No.33 of
2023 and the charge sheet for offence punishable under Section 498A
and 506 of IPC and Section 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act,
1961 before the Indore Bench of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh.
Taking advantage of the situation that in the State of Madhya
Pradesh there are three benches the subsequent case was filed at
Indore by the petitioners mischievously suppressing the dismissal
of similar quash petition by the principle seat at Jabalpur.
5. In the considered opinion of this court as held by the High
Court  vide  order dated 25.09.2024 passed in Misc.Criminal Case
No.17123 of 2023, the FIR certainly contains serious allegations
against the accused persons and the High Court is not supposed to
conduct a trial while deciding the matter under Seton 482 CrPC in
the light of the judgment delivered in the case of… (CITATION) and
therefore, the order passed by the High Court dated 25.09.2024 is
upheld.
6. Insofar as the SLP preferred by the wife is concerned, the
order passed by Indore Bench allowing the second petition filed
under Section 482 CRPC preferred by the husband is set aside and it
is directed that the Court at Kyanmore District Katni will continue
with the trial as the petitioners have not come with clean hands.
7. It is unfortunate that the petitioners have misused the
judicial forum by filing a similar case before two benches and the
bench at Indore has allowed the petitioners’ petition filed under
3

## Page 289

Section 482 CrPC and therefore, this Court is passing a common
order in respect of both the matters.
8. The petitioners in the first SLP i.e., husband and his father
in all fairness should have disclosed the factum of filing the
first petition under Section 482 before the Indore Bench of the
same High Court and in all fairness, should have disclosed this
fact also to this Court. This is nothing but a sheer abuse of a
process of law and an attempt to mislead this Court.
9. Therefore this Court is of the opinion that costs should be
imposed upon the petitioners for misleading this Court and abusing
the process of justice, resultantly a costs of Rs.5,00,000/- is
imposed upon the petitioners. The same shall be paid by the
petitioners within thirty days from today and if the same is not
been paid, it shall be recovered as arrears of land revenue.
10. The Registry of this Court is directed to transmit the costs
so recovered from the petitioners to the Army Battle Casuality
Fund.
11. Special Leave Petitions are disposed of in the aforesaid
terms.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

O R D E R 
 
1. Delay condoned. 
2. Despite a direction to the parties in the appeal before 
the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), who 
were also parties in the Civil Appeal before this Court, to co-
operate with the NCLAT when the proceedings were taken up 
on 18.09.2024 for disposal of the appeal on merits; the matter 
is still pending before the NCLAT.  
3. It is pointed out by the learned Senior Counsel 
appearing for the applicant that the hearing in the matter had 
proceeded considerably and the NCLAT, taking cognizance of 
a later order dated 31.10.2025, directed exchange of 
pleadings. Arguments were commenced by the applicant on 

## Page 303

Page 2 of 3 
 
 
28.01.2026 and concluded on 04.02.2026. The Resolution 
Professional put forth his arguments on 25.02.2026 and the 
Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) concluded the 
arguments on 20.04.2026. However, the Committee of 
Creditors (CoC) sought time, and in the interim period, the 
Hon’ble Member (Judicial) who was hearing the matter in a 
Division Bench, got transferred to Delhi. The new incumbent 
had then posted the hearing on 05.08.2026, which stood 
adjourned to 27.08.2026. The parties only want expeditious 
consideration of the matter.  
4. Considering the fact that the matter would now have to 
be reheard due to the transfer of the Member (Judicial), we 
would think it apposite to direct the constitution of a bench to 
hear the part-heard matter. Though, it has now been removed 
from part-heard, the matter would be restored as a part-heard 
matter and the Registry of the Principal Bench of the NCLAT 
will constitute a Special Bench comprising of the Members of 
the Bench which heard the matter considerably. The hearing 
shall proceed on online mode with the Member (Judicial) 
sitting in Delhi and the Member (Technical) sitting in Chennai.  

## Page 304

Page 3 of 3 
 
 
5. We direct the Registry of the Principal Bench of the 
NCLAT to constitute the bench as directed herein within a 
week from today and fix a date for hearing within two weeks 
therefrom with due notice to the parties. The CoC shall 
positively put forth its arguments on the scheduled date and 
we request the Special Bench constituted to hear the matter on 
a day-to-day basis, if necessary, in the afternoon session and 
conclude the hearing expeditiously. We would also request 
the Special Bench to pass the orders on the same without much 
delay.  
6. The MA stands disposed of with the above direction. 
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                     O R D E R
IA No. 258111/2026 in Crl.A. No. 3228/2025 
1. The present application has been filed by the
appellant, Dharmendra Bariha, seeking grant of bail
during the pendency of the appeal.
2. In the light of the fact that other co-accused
have already been granted bail during the pendency
of their appeal(s), the role by and large of the
appellant is identical to theirs, and the appellant
has  undergone  more  than  eight  years  of  his
sentence, the present application is allowed.
3. The appellant is directed to be released on
bail  during  the  pendency  of  the  appeal  in
connection with Sessions Trial No. 40 of 2018 on
the terms and conditions as may be fixed by the
First Additional Sessions Judge concerned.
4. If the appellant possesses a passport, the
same shall be surrendered before the Competent
Authority or the Court until the disposal of the
appeal, unless directed otherwise.

1. Heard learned counsel for the parties.

read  with  Section  11(12)(a)  of  the  Arbitration  and
Conciliation  Act,  1996,  seeking  appointment  of  a  Sole
Arbitrator to adjudicate the disputes between the parties
arising out of the License Agreement dated 21.05.2018.
3. Having regard to the arbitration agreement contained in
Clause 13 of the License Agreement dated 21.05.2018 and the
fact that the petitioner is a corporation incorporated
outside  India,  constituting  an  international  commercial
arbitration under Section 2(1)(f)(ii) of the Act, we deem it
appropriate to allow this petition.
4. Accordingly,  we  appoint  Hon’ble  Mr.  Justice  Amjad
Ahtesham Sayed, Former Chief Justice of the High Court of
Himachal Pradesh, as the Sole Arbitrator to adjudicate the
disputes and differences between the parties.
5. The seat and venue of the arbitration shall be Mumbai,
India, in terms of Clause 13 of the License Agreement.
6. The learned Sole Arbitrator shall be at liberty to fix
his fees in consultation with the parties.
7. All rights and contentions of the parties on merits,
including issues relating to the scope of the arbitration
agreement and arbitrability of claims, are kept open to be

8. The Arbitration Petition is allowed in the aforesaid
terms.

2. In the impugned order, the Division Bench of the High
Court has recorded the following directions:-
“In the backdrop of the above discussions, this Court
finds that the issue of conferment of notional benefits
with  effect  from  26th February,  1996  following  the
resolution of the Board dated 21st February, 1990 is in
the nature of a policy decision and requires to be
approved by the Ministry/Government in terms of the 1948
Regulations. Accordingly, let there be a direction upon
the Secretary, Ministry of Shipping to take steps upon
consultation with the essential stakeholders, including
the writ petitioners and pass a reasoned order which
shall be communicated to the stakeholders/the concerned
parties.”
3. We enquired from the learned counsel for respondent nos.8
& 9 that whether any reasoned order has been passed? Learned
counsel drew attention to the affidavit filed by respondent
nos.8  &  9  in  this  Court  dated  17.03.2025.  In  the  said
affidavit, apart from stating that upgradation will require the
approval of the Ministry/Government, there is no indication as
to whether pursuant to the directions of the Division Bench of
the High Court any order was made and communicated.
4. That being the position, before proceeding further with
the matter, we direct respondent nos.8 & 9 to comply with the
directions of the Division Bench of the High Court as extracted
hereinabove and pass an order within a period of two months
from today.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 5813 OF 2025
ANSAR ALI APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE REGIONAL MANAGER, NEW 
INDIA ASSURANCE COMPANY LTD.
RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The appellant was doing repair work under a tipper lorry
bearing Registration No.KA-22-A-3127.  While he was so engaged, the
driver of the lorry started the vehicle, and as a result, the jack
came in contact with an electric wire and the appellant suffered
electric shock. Consequently, his left arm from the elbow had to be
amputated and he also suffered burn injuries in his right arm. The
Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) assessed the functional
disability of the appellant at 70% and fixed the compensation at
Rs.11,16,345/-.
2. Being aggrieved, the appellant approached the High Court and
the High Court enhanced the compensation to Rs. 12,44,345/- with
interest @ 6% per annum from the date of the petition till the date
of realization of the amount.
3. We have heard the learned counsel for the parties. We have
also considered the nature of injury suffered by the appellant both
in his left and right hand.  Though, the doctor, PW4, opined that
the disability of the appellant was 70%, in view the nature of
disability suffered by the appellant in both hands, we are of the
opinion such disability would severely impair the appellant's
earning potential to almost 100%.
1

## Page 381

4. Given such aggravated weightage of the appellant’s disability
on his earning potential, we are of the considered view that over
and above the amount awarded by the High Court, the appellant shall
be awarded a sum of Rs. 10 lakhs, which shall be paid within six
weeks from date, in addition to what was awarded by the High Court,
failing which such additional sum shall carry an interest of 9% per
annum till realisation.
5. The appeal stands disposed of, in the above terms.
             
..........................J.
       (JOYMALYA BAGCHI)
..........................J.
       (V. MOHANA) 
           
NEW DELHI;
NOVEMBER 16, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CIVIL) NO.         OF 2026)
DIARY NO.31184 OF 2023
AKSHAY DAS APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
DIVISIONAL MANAGER, NATIONAL 
INSURANCE CO. LTD. & ANR.
RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Leave granted.
3. The appellant had sustained injuries in the course of his
employment as a helper in the truck bearing Registration No.OR-09-
6005. Dr. Anandi Charan Naik, PW-2, opined that the injury had
caused permanent disablement to the extent of 70% and loss of
income of 100%. Relying on such expert opinion, the Commissioner
for  Employee’s  Compensation-cum-Divisional  Labour  Commissioner,
Cuttack, in E.C. Case No. 12-D/2012, awarded compensation to the
tune of 16,01,224/- which was to be paid within 30 days from date₹
of the order, failing which 50% penalty with 12% interest per annum
shall be added to the awarded sum.  
4. On  appeal  by  the  company,  the  High  Court  reduced  the
compensation on an erroneous finding that PW-2 was not a specialist
as  he  had  no  special  knowledge  in  orthopedic  treatment.
Accordingly, the compensation amount was reduced to 6,12,599/-₹
along with 12% interest per annum from the date of accident till
1

## Page 384

the date of deposit made by the insurer before the Commissioner. By
the self-same order, the High Court directed refund of the sum
already deposited with proportionate accrued interest. The amount
of penalty to the extent of 50% was also waived.
5. Having heard the counsel for the parties, we are of the view
the High Court had erred in putting itself in the place of an
expert to assess the disablement and the consequential loss of
income. It is nobody's case that PW-2 is not a qualified and
experienced  doctor.  Whether  he  is  specialized  in  orthopedic
treatment or not is of little consequence.
6. Accordingly, we set aside the order(s) of the High Court and
affirm  the  order  passed  by  the  Commissioner  for  Employee’s
Compensation-cum-Divisional Labour Commissioner, Cuttack, in E.C.
Case No. 12-D/2012. The appeals are allowed. The insurance company
shall release the balance amount within six weeks from today.
             
..........................J.
       (JOYMALYA BAGCHI)
..........................J.
       (V. MOHANA)  
           
NEW DELHI;
NOVEMBER 16, 2026.

For Respondent(s) : 
       UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The  only  ground  raised  in  the  present
transfer petition seeking transfer of proceedings
bearing Criminal Regular Case No.53113 of 2026,
titled  “Karnal  Indranad  Jha  Vs.  Pawan  Kumar
Mishra”,  instituted  under  Section  138  of  the
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, pending before
the  Court  of  the  learned  Special  Judicial
Magistrate  (N.I.  Act),  Kota,  Rajasthan  to  the
learned District Court, Madhubani, Bihar, is that
of inconvenience to the parties.
1

## Page 420

2. In view of the authoritative pronouncement
of this Court in the case of “Shri Sendhur Agro and
Oil Industries Vs. Kotak Mahindra Bank”,  (2025)
INSC 328, the only ground of inconvenience cannot
be  successfully  raised  in  seeking  transfer  of
criminal proceedings.
3. The  relevant  observations  of  the  said
judgment made by this Court is reproduced below:
“…...65. For the purpose of transfer of any
case or proceedings under Section 406 of
the Cr.P.C., the case must fall within the
ambit of the expression “expedient for the
ends  of  justice”.  Mere  inconvenience  or
hardship that the accused may have to face
in travelling from Coimbatore to Chandigarh
would  not  fall  within  the  expression
“expedient for the ends of justice”. The
case  must  fall  within  any  of  the  five
situations as narrated in para 49 of this
judgment.  It  is  always  open  for  the
petitioner accused to pray for exemption
from  personal  appearance  or  request  the
Court that he may be permitted to join the
proceedings online.
66. Having regard to the pleadings in the
memorandum of the transfer petition, we
have reached the conclusion that no case is
made out for transfer of the proceedings in
question under 406 CrPC.
67. In the result, the petition fails and
is hereby dismissed. All other connected
transfer petitions are also disposed of in
the aforesaid terms…..”
4. In view of the above, since the only ground
raised in the present transfer petition is that of
inconvenience, no case is made out for transfer of
the said proceedings.
2

## Page 421

5. Accordingly, the present Transfer Petition
stands rejected.
6. Pending applications shall stand disposed
of. 
      (SOURAV PAL)                    (AJEET SINGH TARIYAL)

and has also filed counter affidavit, no one was
available to contest the transfer petition when the
matter  was  taken  up  by  the  Court.  Four  other
proceedings  arising  from  the  matrimonial  strife
between  the  parties  are  already  pending  before
competent courts at Agra.  
3. In this view of the matter, we find justifiable
grounds to transfer HMA No.2467 of 2025 titled “Ishwar
Singh  vs.  Radha  Rani  Nagar” from  the  Court  of
1

## Page 438

Principal judge, Family Court, North West District,
Rohini Courts, Delhi to the Court of Principal Judge,
Family Court, Agra, Uttar Pradesh.
4. The entire record pertaining to the said case
shall be transmitted forthwith by the transferor court
to the transferee court.
5. The parties are at liberty initially to appear
through virtual mode. If such request is made, the
concerned court may favourably consider the same and
thereafter, if need be, the parties can be asked to
appear through physical mode.
6. Accordingly, the transfer petition is allowed.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. The Special Leave Petitions are directed against the interim
order dated 06.05.2026 passed by the High Court by which the
application for impleadment filed by respondent nos.5 to 12, in a
Writ Petition filed by the petitioner, has been allowed.
3. Mr. Dinesh Dwivedi, learned senior counsel for the petitioner
submits that the subject matter of the petition pertains to the
validity  of  Lucknow  Development  Authority’s  demand  of
Rs. 8.36 crores towards development charges and the reduction of
the adjustment area under the State Policy. It is further submitted
that the presence of respondent nos.5 to 12 is not necessary for
the adjudication of the controversy involved in the petition as the
lis  is  between  the  petitioner  and  the  Lucknow  Development
Authority. On the other hand, learned counsel for the respondents
submits that the order does not call for any interference.
4. We have considered the submissions made on both sides. In the
facts and circumstances of the case, the impugned order does not
warrant any interference. However, the High Court while hearing
respondent nos.5 to 12 shall bear in mind the scope of the Writ
Petition and the reliefs prayed for by the petitioner in the Writ
Petition.
5. We have not expressed any opinion on the merits of the matter.
6. Accordingly, the Special Leave Petitions are disposed of.
2

## Page 747

agreement of sale between the decree-holder(s) and petitioner’s father and the
consideration was alleged and linked to the outcome of the litigation, i.e., 20%
above the market value, if the decree-holder(s) succeeds and 15% below the
market value, if it is otherwise. This story is the basis to ignite proceedings
Order XXI Rule 97 of the CPC and to contend that said application, which has
since been dismissed by both Courts ought to have been adjudicated by the
trial court by recording the oral evidence. Said contention is contrary to the very
statutory provision itself. There is no straight-jacket formula under Order XXI
Rule 97 of the CPC that would mandate recording of evidence when such claims
are raised. Here, in the instant case, it is the original judgment-debtor, who has
set up his son, to ignite these proceedings to stave off the decree which has
received the imprimatur of this Court way back on 02.02.2024 passed in Special
Leave  Petition  (Civil)  No.2257/2024.  The  decree-holder(s)  is  still  unable  to
secure the possession of the suit schedule premises to which a decree came to
be passed on 25.03.2010 which arose out of a suit filed in Regular Civil Suit
No.533/1991.  The  saga  of  obtaining  possession  not  having  fructified  still
continues and as such we direct the Executing Court to forthwith depute a
Special Bailiff to execute the decree, if necessary, through police help and for
break open the lock, if any, put up on the schedule premises and deliver the
possession  under  appropriate  Mahazar  to  the  decree-holder(s)  expeditiously
and at any rate within an outer limit of six weeks from today.
3. A report in a sealed cover shall be forwarded by the Executing Court to
this court through proper channel in this regard.
4. List on 05.01.2027.

1. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and in view of
the fact that the dispute is pending for more than three decades,
we invoke our powers under Article 142 of the Constitution and
direct that a consolidated sum of Rs.10 lakhs over and above amount
fixed by the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, New

failing  which  it  shall  carry  an  interest  of  9%  p.a.  till
realisation.

APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
NEW INDIA ASSURANCE CO. LTD. &
ANR.
RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. We have considered the submissions of the parties.  Though, we
are of the view that the flooding did not directly contribute to
the loss or damage covered under the Policy, it cannot be ruled out
that such flooding may have had a contributory role in the damage
so caused.  Giving a liberal interpretation to the terms of the
Policy, we are inclined to direct the insurance company to pay a
sum of Rs.1.50 crores as compensation to the appellant within six
weeks from date failing which the amount shall carry an interest @
9% p.a. till realisation.
2. The appeal stands disposed of, in the above terms.

O R D E R
1. We have considered the materials on record.  We are not in
agreement with the findings of the National Consumer Disputes
Redressal  Commission  (“Commission”)  that  as  the  accident  had
occurred during the testing of the machine, the same shall not be
covered by the insurance policy.
2. But keeping in mind the fact that the parties are litigating
for over a decade, we are not inclined to remand the matter for
fresh consideration by the Tribunal and by invoking our powers
under Article 142 of the Constitution, we direct the insurance
company to pay a compensation of Rs.1.75 crores within six weeks
from date failing which the amount shall carry an interest @ 9%
p.a. till realisation.
3. The appeal stands disposed of, in the above terms.

        UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                          O R D E R
1. The petitioner has been convicted for the offence under
Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and has been
directed to pay compensation to the tune of Rs. 21,40,000/- (Rupees
Twenty One Lakh and Forty Thousand Only) to the respondent no.
1/complainant with sentence of imprisonment, upon default to pay
compensation.
2. Three Courts have returned concurrent findings against the
petitioner, convicting him for the above offence and awarding
compensation as above.
3. The petitioner has deposited a sum of Rs.4,00,000/-(Rupees
Four Lakh Only) in the High Court.  Today, learned counsel for the

## Page 881

petitioner submits that the petitioner is ready to deposit another
sum of Rs. 2,00,000/-(Rupees Two Lakh Only) in this Court.
4. Learned counsel for the respondent has opposed the submissions
so advanced.  It is submitted that the cheque was for a sum of Rs.
20,00,000/-(Rupees Twenty Lakh Only) and the petitioner having
suffered concurrent findings of conviction by three Courts, is not
entitled to the benefit of exemption from surrendering.
5. Prima  facie,  this  Court  finds  merit  in  the  submissions
advanced by learned counsel for the respondent.
6. In the peculiar facts noted above and to balance the equities,
the petitioner is given indulgence of exemption from surrender,
subject to his depositing a sum of Rs. 10,00,000/-(Rupees Ten Lakh
Only) in the Registry of this Court on or before 07.12.2026. The
sum  of  Rs.  2,00,000/-(Rupees  Two  Lakh  Only)  offered  by  the
petitioner as above will be adjusted in this amount.
7. Till then, the petitioner shall be exempted from surrendering.
8. The matter shall be listed in the Court on 14.12.2026.
